Back: God creates the world, humanity falls into sin, and God begins His covenant plan of redemption through Abraham and his descendants, promising blessing, offspring, land, and ultimately a coming deliverer.
God redeems Israel from slavery in Egypt, makes covenant with them at Sinai, gives His law, and dwells among them in the tabernacle as their holy covenant Lord.
The holy God teaches His redeemed people how sinful people may dwell in His presence through sacrifice, priesthood, cleansing, holiness, and atonement.
Israel repeatedly rebels and fails to trust God in the wilderness, yet God remains faithful to His covenant promises and preserves a new generation to enter the promised land.
Moses renews the covenant with Israel before they enter Canaan, calling them to love and obey the LORD wholeheartedly while warning of judgment for rebellion and promising restoration after exile.
God faithfully gives Israel the promised land under Joshua, demonstrating both His judgment on sin and His covenant faithfulness while calling Israel to wholehearted obedience.
Israel repeatedly abandons the LORD, suffers oppression, cries for rescue, and is delivered through flawed judges, revealing the nation’s deep need for a righteous king.
God providentially works through the covenant faithfulness of Ruth and Boaz to preserve the family line that leads to David and ultimately to the Messiah.
Israel transitions from judges to monarchy as God rejects Saul’s disobedient kingship and raises up David, the king after His own heart, through whom His purposes will advance.
David’s kingdom is established and God promises him an enduring dynasty, but David’s sin and its consequences reveal the need for a greater and perfectly righteous Son of David.
Solomon builds the temple and Israel reaches great prosperity, but idolatry divides the kingdom and both Israel and Judah begin a downward course of covenant unfaithfulness.
Despite repeated prophetic warnings, Israel and Judah persist in idolatry and covenant rebellion until God sends both kingdoms into exile, while preserving hope through the Davidic line.
Israel’s history is retold with special emphasis on David, the temple, worship, and God’s covenant promises, encouraging the restored community to center its life on faithful worship of the LORD.
The history of Judah’s kings and temple shows that seeking the LORD brings blessing while persistent covenant unfaithfulness brings exile, yet the book ends with hope of restoration.
God sovereignly restores a remnant from exile to Jerusalem to rebuild the temple and renew covenant faithfulness through the ministry of Ezra.
God enables Jerusalem’s walls to be rebuilt and the covenant community to be reordered around His law, while exposing the people’s continuing need for deeper spiritual renewal.
Though God is never named, His providence preserves His covenant people from destruction in Persia and reverses the schemes of their enemies.

The suffering of righteous Job explores the mystery of undeserved suffering, rejecting simplistic explanations and calling people to trust the wisdom and sovereignty of God beyond what they can understand.
Israel’s inspired songs teach God’s people to worship, lament, repent, trust, and hope in the LORD and in His anointed King through every circumstance of life.
True wisdom begins with the fear of the LORD and applies God-centered moral insight to speech, work, money, relationships, sexuality, discipline, and the ordinary choices of life.
Life under the sun is fleeting and unable to provide lasting meaning apart from God, so people should fear God, receive His gifts gratefully, and keep His commandments.
The Song celebrates the goodness, delight, exclusivity, and covenant faithfulness of marital love between a man and a woman.
The Holy One of Israel judges His sinful people and the nations, yet promises salvation through the coming Davidic King and suffering Servant who will bear sin and bring a new creation.
Judah’s persistent covenant rebellion makes judgment and exile unavoidable, yet God promises a new covenant in which He will forgive His people and write His law on their hearts.
Jerusalem’s destruction is mourned as the just consequence of sin, yet amid terrible judgment the prophet clings to the LORD’s compassion, faithfulness, and hope of restoration.
God judges Jerusalem and the nations for sin and vindicates His holy name, yet promises to gather, cleanse, regenerate, and shepherd His people and dwell with them again.
God sovereignly rules over earthly kingdoms, preserves His faithful servants in exile, and promises an everlasting kingdom that will ultimately be given to the Son of Man and His saints.
Hosea’s troubled marriage portrays Israel’s spiritual adultery, while God’s persistent covenant love promises judgment, restoration, and renewed relationship with His unfaithful people.
A devastating locust plague foreshadows the day of the LORD, calling God’s people to repentance while promising restoration, the outpouring of God’s Spirit, and final deliverance.
God condemns Israel’s injustice, hypocrisy, and complacency, warning that covenant privilege will not prevent judgment while promising eventual restoration of David’s fallen kingdom.
God judges proud Edom for violence against Judah and promises that the day of the LORD will bring justice on the nations and establish the LORD’s kingdom.
God sends a reluctant prophet to Nineveh to display His sovereign compassion toward repentant sinners among the nations and to expose Jonah’s narrow and self-righteous heart.
God indicts Israel and Judah for idolatry, injustice, and corrupt leadership, yet promises forgiveness, restoration, and a ruler from Bethlehem who will shepherd His people in peace.
God announces the certain destruction of violent and arrogant Nineveh, comforting His oppressed people with the truth that the LORD is both just and a refuge for those who trust Him.
The prophet wrestles with how a holy God can use wicked Babylon to judge Judah and learns that the righteous must live by faith while awaiting God’s certain justice.
The coming day of the LORD will bring sweeping judgment on Judah and the nations, yet God will preserve and rejoice over a humble remnant whom He restores.
Haggai calls the returned exiles to put God first by rebuilding the temple and encourages them with the promise that God is with them and greater glory is still to come.
Through visions and prophecies, God encourages the restored community to repent and rebuild while promising a coming humble King, a pierced shepherd, cleansing from sin, and the LORD’s final reign.
God confronts post-exilic Israel’s corrupt worship and covenant unfaithfulness and promises that the Lord and His messenger will come to purify, judge, and restore His people.
